A test is only valuable if it actually fails when the behavior it claims to cover is broken. Several reviews caught tests that looked thorough but were vacuous: a chained `.should` assertion that short-circuits on `undefined` instead of failing (use `should(value).deepEqual(...)` form), a relative comparison ("less than 20x") that passes even if caching or flat-rate pricing is subtly wrong, a fixture that defaults an unset env var to a hardcoded number instead of leaving it genuinely unset, or a helper that only exercises the "listed" branch and never asserts the "unlisted" branch actually excludes the id. Prefer asserting the precise invariant (exact equality between two differently-sized payloads, exact set of rejected fields, exact signal sent) over a loose bound, and when a bug is fixed, write the test against the pre-fix code first to confirm it fails, then confirm it passes after the fix — this mutation-style sanity check should be part of the review description. Where feasible, exercise the real code path instead of a fully mocked one (a real adapter with a stubbed fetch, a real platform's native module, a real subprocess startup, a real script run against a temp directory with symlinks) since mocks can hide integration bugs that only appear against the real implementation. Derive expected values from the single source of truth (e.g. compare an exported constant against the actual `package.json`) rather than duplicating a literal that can drift. At the same time, don't over-invest: once the core behavioral contract is covered by a few sharp cases, skip tests that would only pin incidental implementation details (internal telemetry phase sequencing, exact log line shape) where existing coverage already catches real regressions — that churn isn't worth the harness it requires.
